title: The Greatness of John the Baptist
english: He manifested glory, he revealed the glory of the only-begotten.
Let John be hymned, the flute-player of whose song all run.
For who hearing does not repent?
Who does not hasten to wash?
Who does not desire to be cleansed?
Who does not bring a vessel to the spring to draw, to drink, and to cool the burner, wishing?
Who, having learned that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near, does not desire to reach his brother first, and does not hasten to take the neighbor before?
Let John be hymned, whose first wonders and last are great and exceedingly radiant.
The first wonders: Gabriel announced to him his birth, an angel interpreted the conception to Zachariah.
From heaven the gift stood between the temple and the altar, the priest received it, and the cowardly sons of the Jews obtained so much.
For there the priest of God received the announcement, there they sharpen the sword and arm the hands and practice murder and work the drama.
What then did Gabriel say to Zachariah?
'Do not fear, Zachariah, because your supplication has been heard, and behold, your wife Elizabeth will bear a son to you, and you shall call his name John.'
And there will be for you joy and exultation, and many will rejoice at his birth.

For he will be great before the Lord, and he will not drink wine or strong drink at all, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb, and he will turn back many of the sons of Israel to the Lord their God.

He will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, turning the hearts of fathers back to their children and leading the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, to prepare a people fit for the Lord. You should consider the great honor bestowed on John the Baptist even before his birth, for he becomes a source of blessing before his very conception.

Do not be afraid, Zacharias, for the Redeemer is coming and the people will cease from sin. Your prayer has been heard. Now is the time when heaven and earth must bow to receive their Creator. And behold, your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son.

The barren woman gives birth, so that the Virgin may have a ground for the wonder and become the God-bearer. And you will call his name John: fittingly the name is strange, since the thing to which the name is given is strange too. The name is new, for new is the mystery to be fulfilled through him. And you will have joy and gladness: joy because you bear this one of whom it is said that among those born of women none is greater, and gladness because the end of the law and the prophets will come through him, the one born of you. And many will rejoice at his birth, those who accept his message of repentance and are cleansed in the bath of baptism. But the scribes do not rejoice, and the Pharisees mourn with them. To these he declares the winnowing fan and the axe, threatening and proclaiming the cutting down, for which reasons the forest has existed to them as thorny, wood-mad, beast-like, and inhumane. What then is the other by which Gabriel dignifies the Baptist, having announced?

He will be great in the sight of the Lord, for he points out the Lamb of God who bears the sin of the whole world; yet his greatness is defined not by heavenly stature as humans measure it, but by his divine orientation. Indeed, while Jews may find laughter in the mysteries of Christ, they mock the heralds of truth, treating the very proclaimers of grace as enemies and comic figures.

He shall drink neither wine nor strong drink, lest the spirit destined to dwell in him be constricted; for he is to be filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb—not merely receiving the gift in advance or anticipating the graces, but so that he may proclaim the light before addressing it, announce the Maker before beholding His own elements, denounce the sun before witnessing its daily course, and having watched the night’s extremities.

And many of the sons of Israel he will turn back to the Lord their God, for he was the great teacher of Andrew, and this one had served as instructor to John the theologian before they brought themselves to the net. From him the apostles learned: 'Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' and 'Rabbi, where do you dwell?' as they followed him, eager to enter the tent of the Uncontainable.

He will go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah, not in soul and body. Away, away from absurdity. Yet the sons of Greeks idle talk and mythologize, claiming souls pre-exist and pass from body to body, just as the mentally disturbed utter their words against them.

title: The Forerunner’s Solitary Witness
english: They seek the redundant and the herded. Yet to each soul the Creator has given a distinct body, whence John, though called a second Elijah and spoken of due to zeal toward him, is nevertheless not in soul and body; but the One who has given spiritual energy to that one, this same One also grants to John the Baptist and forerunner a measure of gift, just as that one received. The One who supplied power to the ancient promises to supply it to the new.

He will turn back the hearts of fathers to the children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just. 'Fathers' refers to Israel, 'children' to the nations by the course of time; yet the fathers turn back to the children, for the children draw near the fountain of life, and they take hold of the banquet of joy as those who are wise and faithful, and having taken the table of light in advance, they encircle it. Thus those called 'fathers' are rightly named 'disobedient', for concerning them Isaiah the prophet has proclaimed: 'I know that you are stubborn, and your neck is an iron sinew, and your forehead is bronze,' that the inflexibility of the synagogue and the utter disobedience of its heirs may be explained. But 'the just' are those from the nations; for if they once barely knew justice, now they pursue it with diligence; if they did not know the door of godliness, now they run into the bridal chamber with joy, entering therein; if they were once far from the light, now they behold the whole sun with pure eyes.

Why does Gabriel, in fulfilling another promise, declare, 'To prepare for the Lord a people made ready'? Who made them ready, if not Christ? For the One who formed also raised up; the One who set the wheel in motion from the beginning, this One later unrolled it. The One who said, 'Let a living soul come into being,' this One spoke; 'I do not wish the sinner to perish.' And these things, Gabriel, descending from heaven, proclaimed. In those words, John leaped within Elizabeth's womb and came to be; taking the One in the womb, he greets from the womb, and the One in the womb still theologizes, bound by the womb's bonds, while being held fast. Then, born, he is sent into the wilderness, that he may be like the wild beasts, that he may converse with God, that he may become free from the smokes and tumults of labors, that he may practice courage, that he may be instructed by the sensible beasts what manner they need to box the hidden ones and to fight against those who lurk. With age advancing and time progressing, he becomes a dinner guest at a table lacking a cook, not even hiring one; for wild honey was his food, completely unseasoned, and locusts were his food, of which the sacrifice was impious, the slaughter of goats unprofitable, needing no coals; he had no need of an external oven, but he acquired the oven from himself; and camel's hairs clothed the Baptist, that the spirit might warm the shivering body, and the melting flesh might cause the worms of pleasures to die; but also a leather girdle he wore around his loins.

He dwelt apart, sustained not by the craft of kitchens nor the hire of cooks, but by what the wilderness freely gave: honey untouched by art, locusts untouched by altar or slaughter, needing neither fire nor fuel. His garment was of camel's hair, girt with leather, not for show but to warm the frame and chill the flesh, that the worms of delight might perish in the melting. Thus he lived, not as one who prepares meals, but as one whose life itself became the preparation.
The mortification of pleasures shone brighter than gold; the sanctification flashed like electrum; the purity of many-shining stones concealed their radiant beams.

Thus, having practiced philosophy, the true ascetic was made complete — a guileless runner, a blameless soldier, a just leader of brides, a pious herald, a mediator, a forerunner, one who keeps himself from every sort of evil deed.
How often did the devil, seeing him philosophize thus, envy him? Yet he had no power to slander.

And what, being exceedingly thirsty, longing, and in need? What then — to slander the athlete, to mock the soldier, to jeer at the one who holds nothing in his hands? What prosperity could one proclaim of him who has no kinship to the well-being of life?

He had no children to slander, for he did not sow them; no daughters, since he did not obtain a father; no fields, for he did not possess them; no houses, since he did not raise them; no donkeys, oxen, or camels, for he acquired none; no woman, whom he did not know, did not have, did not marry.
Let John therefore be hymned — again I say — since to all he imparted beneficially the proclamation of preservation.

title: Baptism of Jesus
english: As they were bringing and supplying what was needed, the people hastened to the fountain of baptism, and the Redeemer himself wanted to follow them like a shepherd with sheep, to participate in the fountain which he had shown to the lambs.
The Baptist's fingers were striking, his hands were numb, each of his limbs was trembling from head to foot.
The Savior said to the Baptist, 'I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me.'

The Baptist asked, 'How can I cleanse the clean one? How can I grasp the uncontainable one? How can I whiten light? How can I anoint the sun?' He wondered what his hand needed, what word he needed to say while baptizing, what he would say to the Jordan, to the dove from heaven, to the cloud which proclaims the message of his Father, and what he would say to you, baptizing?
The Baptist asked if the Savior was unaware of what he was, or why he had come.
The Savior replied, 'Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness (Matthew 3:15).'

The Baptist asked if he had been conceived in iniquities, or if his mother had conceived him in sins, if his birth was corruption or if his conception was a mixture, if the womb was a bride or the belly a farmer, if milk came from a man, if someone had touched his mother's breast, or if the Virgin had fallen under the curse of Eve.
Let go now, what are you doing to those who are not yet ready, what are you revealing that should still be hidden??
You are disturbing the Jews and shooting at the devil's ears, driving away the demons from the earth before the cross, and making the servants of the cross sacrifice against their will.
Let go now, what are you doing to yourself, what are you depriving your nature of?
If I am not baptized, how will I hear the voice of God, and if I do not hear the voice, how will I learn the Father's plan and be confident in the Son's mysteries?
I was born of a woman and paid the debt of Eve, I took the form of a servant and freed Adam from debt, I sat on a manger and the one who became beastly is freed from curse and shame.

I wore swaddling clothes and healed the wound of nakedness, I was circumcised for the sake of Israel, and now I am baptized again for the nations, and thus all righteousness is sealed to my laws and works.
Emboldened by the ministry of the mystery and the vision of the dove, he became even more confident and acquired a more radiant boldness, speaking out against tyrants and rebuking the lawless Herod.
With the voice of the Father, he spoke to the king with a loud voice, saying, 'It is not lawful for you to have the wife of Philip your brother (Leviticus 18:16, 20:21).'
If you do not keep the law, you will not be able to hold the scepter.
If you transgress the commandment, you must take off the purple.
If you despise God, you must come down from the throne you took from him.
He warned the king not to be proud of his arms, for the laws protect the king.
He urged him not to neglect virtue, for it is more honorable than the golden throne.
Again, he said, 'It is not lawful for you to have the wife of Philip your brother.'
He pleaded with him to spare the succession of his family and not to corrupt the order of the royal seed.

He asked, 'Whose child will the one born from Herodias, who was corrupted by you, be called, the former husband's or the second adulterer's, the one who lawfully mounted the bed or the one who unlawfully seized it? Shall we call the son born from her Philip's?'
The one born from her is a stranger to him.
